questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Rearrange the following propositions into a valid syllogism:

No reptiles are hot-blooded animals; No hot-blooded animals are lizards; All lizards are reptiles. (3 marks)

(ii) Give the Mood and Figure of a (i) above. (2 marks)

(iii) Prove the validity of a (i) above by the Venn Diagram Technique. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The valid arrangement.**

The three propositions use three terms: reptiles, hot-blooded animals, lizards. Only one choice of conclusion gives a valid syllogism (this was checked by testing the three possible choices with Python). The conclusion is **"No hot-blooded animals are lizards"**. Then:

- the **major term** (predicate of the conclusion) is *lizards*, and the major premise is the one that contains it: *All lizards are reptiles*;
- the **minor term** (subject of the conclusion) is *hot-blooded animals*, and the minor premise is *No reptiles are hot-blooded animals*;
- the **middle term** is *reptiles* (it appears in both premises, not in the conclusion).

> All lizards are reptiles. (major premise)
> No reptiles are hot-blooded animals. (minor premise)
> Therefore, no hot-blooded animals are lizards. (conclusion)

The two other choices fail: with "All lizards are reptiles" as conclusion both premises would be negative (E, E), and nothing follows from two negative premises; with "No reptiles are hot-blooded animals" as conclusion the premises give the form EAE-4, which commits the fallacy of the illicit minor (the minor term "reptiles" is undistributed in the premise, as predicate of an A proposition, but distributed in the conclusion).

**(ii) Mood and figure.**

- Major premise: *All $P$ are $M$*, an **A** proposition. Minor premise: *No $M$ are $S$*, an **E** proposition. Conclusion: *No $S$ are $P$*, an **E** proposition. **Mood: AEE.**
- The middle term is the predicate of the major premise and the subject of the minor premise (pattern $P$-$M$, $M$-$S$): **Figure 4.**

The syllogism is **AEE-4** (mnemonic name **Camenes**).

**(iii) Proof by the Venn diagram technique.**

Draw three overlapping circles: $R$ (reptiles), $H$ (hot-blooded animals), $L$ (lizards). The overlaps give eight regions (listed below). Represent the **universal premises first** by shading the empty regions.

1. Premise 1, *All lizards are reptiles*: the part of $L$ outside $R$ is empty, so shade it (regions 3 and 6).
2. Premise 2, *No reptiles are hot-blooded animals*: the overlap of $R$ and $H$ is empty, so shade it (regions 4 and 7).

| Region of the three circles | Reptiles $R$ | Hot-blooded $H$ | Lizards $L$ | Status |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | yes | no | no | free |
| 2 | no | yes | no | free |
| 3 | no | no | yes | **shaded** by premise 1 (a lizard that is not a reptile) |
| 4 | yes | yes | no | **shaded** by premise 2 (reptile and hot-blooded) |
| 5 | yes | no | yes | free |
| 6 | no | yes | yes | **shaded** by premise 1 (a lizard that is not a reptile) |
| 7 | yes | yes | yes | **shaded** by premise 2 (reptile and hot-blooded) |
| 8 (outside the circles) | no | no | no | free |

Now read the diagram for the conclusion *No hot-blooded animals are lizards*: the overlap of $H$ and $L$ is made of regions 6 and 7, and **both are already shaded** by the premises. The conclusion is therefore contained in the premises without any further drawing, and the syllogism is **valid**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(iii) Prove the validity of a (i) above by the use of General rule. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The syllogism of a (i) is: *All lizards are reptiles; No reptiles are hot-blooded animals; therefore no hot-blooded animals are lizards* (AEE-4). It is tested against the general rules of the categorical syllogism.

1. **Three terms only, each used in the same sense**: lizards, reptiles, hot-blooded animals. Satisfied.
2. **The middle term (reptiles) is distributed at least once**: it is the predicate of an A proposition in the major premise (undistributed), but the **subject of an E proposition** in the minor premise (distributed). Satisfied.
3. **No term is distributed in the conclusion unless it is distributed in its premise**: the conclusion is E, so both its terms are distributed. *Lizards* is the subject of the A major premise (distributed); *hot-blooded animals* is the predicate of the E minor premise (distributed). Satisfied.
4. **Two negative premises prove nothing**: only the minor premise is negative. Satisfied.
5. **If one premise is negative the conclusion must be negative, and if the conclusion is negative one premise must be negative**: one premise (E) is negative and the conclusion (E) is negative. Satisfied.
6. **Particular premises**: both premises are universal, and the conclusion is universal, so no rule about particulars is broken.

Every general rule is observed, so the syllogism is **valid**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the statement: *Either Mary is a teacher or a student*

(i) Construct a *Modus Ponendo Tollens* argument. (3 marks)

(ii) Why is b (i) considered an invalid form of the Disjunctive Argument? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $T$ = Mary is a teacher, $S$ = Mary is a student. The statement is the disjunction $T \vee S$.

**(i) A Modus Ponendo Tollens argument.**

*Modus ponendo tollens* means "the mode that, by **affirming** (ponendo), **denies** (tollens)": one alternative of the disjunction is affirmed in the minor premise and the other is denied in the conclusion.

> Either Mary is a teacher or Mary is a student.
> Mary is a teacher.
> Therefore, Mary is not a student.

Form: $T \vee S,\ T\ \therefore\ \sim S$.

**(ii) Why it is an invalid form of the disjunctive argument.**

The "or" of ordinary logic (the *weak* or *inclusive* disjunction, $\vee$) is true when **at least one**, and possibly **both**, of its alternatives are true. Mary can very well be a teacher **and** a student (a teacher may also be studying part-time). So the premises can be true while the conclusion is false: with $T$ true and $S$ true, "$T \vee S$" and "$T$" are true but "$\sim S$" is false. This counter-example (checked with Python) shows that the argument is **invalid**: it commits the **fallacy of affirming a disjunct**.

The valid form of the disjunctive argument is the **modus tollendo ponens**: by **denying** one alternative, one **affirms** the other ($T \vee S,\ \sim T\ \therefore\ S$). The modus ponendo tollens would be valid only if the disjunction were **exclusive** (strong: "either ... or ..., but not both"), which the statement does not say.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Paraphrase and symbolise the following:

(i) If John is a pilot then Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver. It is true that Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver. Therefore John is a pilot.

(ii) Either Mary is a nurse or John is a pilot. Mary is not a nurse. Therefore it is true that John is a pilot.

(iii) John is either a pilot or Paul is a driver. Paul is a driver. Therefore John is not a pilot.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Statement letters: $J$ = John is a pilot, $M$ = Mary is a nurse, $D$ = Paul is a driver.

**(i) Paraphrase:** *If John is a pilot, then (Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver). Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver. Therefore, John is a pilot.*

Symbolisation: $J \supset (M \cdot D),\ \ M \cdot D\ \ \therefore\ J$.

This is a hypothetical (mixed) argument that **affirms the consequent**: an invalid form (fallacy of affirming the consequent). Counter-example: $J$ false, $M$ and $D$ true (both premises true, conclusion false).

**(ii) Paraphrase:** *Either Mary is a nurse or John is a pilot. Mary is not a nurse. Therefore, John is a pilot.*

Symbolisation: $M \vee J,\ \ \sim M\ \ \therefore\ J$.

This is the **disjunctive syllogism** (*modus tollendo ponens*), a **valid** form: no row of the truth table makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

**(iii) Paraphrase:** *Either John is a pilot or Paul is a driver. Paul is a driver. Therefore, John is not a pilot.*

Symbolisation: $J \vee D,\ \ D\ \ \therefore\ \sim J$.

This is the *modus ponendo tollens*, which **affirms a disjunct**. With the ordinary (inclusive) "or" it is **invalid** (counter-example: $J$ and $D$ both true). It would be valid only if the disjunction were exclusive.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(c) Identify and explain the following arguments:

(i) If John is a pilot then Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver. It is true that Mary is a nurse and Paul is a driver. Therefore John is a pilot.

(ii) Either Mary is a nurse or John is a pilot. Mary is not a nurse. Therefore it is true that John is a pilot.

(iii) John is either a pilot or Paul is a driver. Paul is a driver. Therefore John is not a pilot. (2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A hypothetical (mixed hypothetical) argument that affirms the consequent.** The major premise is a conditional ($J \supset (M \cdot D)$), the minor premise affirms its **consequent** ($M \cdot D$), and the conclusion affirms the antecedent ($J$). Affirming the consequent is an **invalid** form (the *fallacy of affirming the consequent*): a conditional says that the antecedent is sufficient for the consequent, not that it is necessary, so the consequent may be true for another reason (Mary can be a nurse and Paul a driver although John is not a pilot).

**(ii) A disjunctive syllogism in the mode *modus tollendo ponens*.** The major premise is a disjunction ($M \vee J$), the minor premise **denies** one alternative ($\sim M$) and the conclusion **affirms** the other ($J$). It is **valid**: if at least one alternative is true and one is false, the other must be true.

**(iii) A disjunctive argument in the mode *modus ponendo tollens*.** The major premise is a disjunction ($J \vee D$), the minor premise **affirms** one alternative ($D$) and the conclusion **denies** the other ($\sim J$). With the ordinary inclusive "or" it is **invalid** (the *fallacy of affirming a disjunct*), because both alternatives can be true together; it is valid only for an exclusive disjunction.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Determine whether the following statement forms are tautology, contradiction and contingent.

(i) $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$

(ii) $(P \cdot Q) \cdot (\sim Q \vee \sim P)$

(iii) $\sim [R \vee (Q \equiv P)]$
questions.corrige_markdown:
A statement form is a **tautology** if it is true under every assignment of truth values (all T in the final column), a **contradiction** if it is false under every assignment (all F), and **contingent** if it is true under some assignments and false under others.

**(i)** $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P \cdot Q$ | $P \vee Q$ | $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T |

All T: **tautology** (if both are true, then at least one is true).

**(ii)** $(P \cdot Q) \cdot (\sim Q \vee \sim P)$

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P \cdot Q$ | $\sim Q \vee \sim P$ | $(P \cdot Q) \cdot (\sim Q \vee \sim P)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | F | T | F |
| F | F | F | T | F |

All F: **contradiction** (the form asserts that $P \cdot Q$ is true and that its negation, $\sim Q \vee \sim P$, is true as well).

**(iii)** $\sim [R \vee (Q \equiv P)]$

| $R$ | $Q$ | $P$ | $Q \equiv P$ | $R \vee (Q \equiv P)$ | $\sim [R \vee (Q \equiv P)]$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | T | F |
| T | T | F | F | T | F |
| T | F | T | F | T | F |
| T | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | T | T | T | T | F |
| F | T | F | F | F | T |
| F | F | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | F | T | T | F |

T in two rows and F in the other six: **contingent** (true only when $R$ is false and $Q$ and $P$ have different truth values).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(d) Explain why the following statement are either state are tautology, contradiction and contingent. (3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
*The statements are not printed in this alternative; the three statement forms of the main part (d) are taken: (i) $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$, (ii) $(P \cdot Q) \cdot (\sim Q \vee \sim P)$, (iii) $\sim [R \vee (Q \equiv P)]$.*

A statement form is classified by the **final column of its truth table**, which gives its truth value under every possible assignment to its statement letters.

- **Tautology**: the column contains **only T**; the form is true by its logical form alone, whatever the facts.
- **Contradiction**: the column contains **only F**; the form is false by its logical form alone.
- **Contingent**: the column contains **both T and F**; its truth depends on the facts.

**(i)** $(P \cdot Q) \supset (P \vee Q)$ is a **tautology**: the final column is T in all four rows, because whenever $P \cdot Q$ is true, $P \vee Q$ is true too, and a conditional with a false antecedent is true.

**(ii)** $(P \cdot Q) \cdot (\sim Q \vee \sim P)$ is a **contradiction**: the final column is F in all four rows, because $\sim Q \vee \sim P$ is the negation of $P \cdot Q$ and a statement cannot be true together with its own negation.

**(iii)** $\sim [R \vee (Q \equiv P)]$ is **contingent**: the final column is T in two rows ($R$ false and $Q$, $P$ of different truth values) and F in the six others.

The full tables are those of the main part (d).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Translate this statement into logical notations of propositional functions using the suggested annotations:

Few beasts are human beings (Hx : x is human beings ; Bx : x is a beast) (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In traditional and symbolic logic *"Few $B$ are $H$"* is read as the **conjunction of a particular affirmative and a particular negative**: some beasts are human beings, and some beasts are not (the "few" are those that are, the others are not).

$$(\exists x)(Bx \cdot Hx) \cdot (\exists x)(Bx \cdot \sim Hx)$$

Read: *There is at least one $x$ such that $x$ is a beast and $x$ is a human being, and there is at least one $x$ such that $x$ is a beast and $x$ is not a human being.* (Strictly, "few" also suggests that the beasts that are human beings are a small part of the beasts, a quantity that first-order notation does not express.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
**ALTERNATIVE FOR THE VISUALLY IMPAIRED CANDIDATES ONLY**

(e) What do you understand by truth-functor as used in symbolic logic? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown: A **truth-functor** (truth-functional connective or operator) is a logical symbol that forms a compound statement from one or more statements in such a way that the **truth value of the compound is completely determined by the truth values of its components**. In symbolic logic the truth-functors are negation ($\sim$), conjunction ($\cdot$), disjunction ($\vee$), the conditional ($\supset$) and the biconditional ($\equiv$); each is defined by its truth table. Example: $P \cdot Q$ is true only when $P$ and $Q$ are both true, whatever $P$ and $Q$ mean.
